item.title: PFASST-BISICLES: A Parallel-in-Time Ice Sheet Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.28434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficiently simulating ice sheet dynamics on modern computational systems is essential for projecting the response of ice sheets to climate forcing and the resulting contributions to sea level change. On modern computational systems, this demands high levels of parallelism to fully exploit modern architectures. Traditionally, time-dependent simulations like ice sheet models achieve parallelism entirely by distributing the spatial domain, while remaining serial in time, as solutions are marched forward. We present PFASST-BISICLES, which combines the Parallel Full Approximation Scheme in Space and Time (PFASST) with BISICLES ice sheet model to integrate multiple timesteps concurrently. We evaluate numerical agreement and parallel performance using a fully grounded sinusoidal ice stream with adaptive mesh refinement and the MISMIP+ marine ice-sheet benchmark. For the sinusoidal stream, PFASST-BISICLES produces temporal errors approximately an order of magnitude smaller than forward Euler at the same timestep, although both methods exhibit approximately first-order convergence. Spatial scaling levels off near 16 processors, while temporal parallelism provides further acceleration, with nearly linear speedup through approximately 16 temporal processors. In MISMIP+, PFASST-BISICLES reproduces the main thickness and velocity patterns after glacier evolution of 50 years, with the largest differences concentrated near the grounding zone. Increasing the temporal processor count from one to four, with four spatial processors fixed, reduces runtime from 33.8 to 10.5 hours. These results demonstrate that temporal parallelism can complement spatial decomposition in ice-sheet modeling, reducing time to solution while maintaining agreement in the main simulated features.
item.dc:creator: Weijia (Emma), Liu, Hans Johansen, Daniel F. Martin

item.title: Monogenic signal analysis for wavefield characterisation in distributed acoustic sensing
item.description: arXiv:2611.29757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spatio-temporal wavefield sampled by distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) contains intertwined information about signal strength, oscillatory structure and propagation. We introduce a methodology to disentangle these properties, with applications to the analysis of weak arrivals obscured by noise or stronger wave trains. The method is based on the monogenic signal, a two-dimensional extension of the analytic signal defined via the Riesz transform. In DAS, the monogenic signal decomposes locally dominant arrivals into their amplitude, phase and apparent slowness along the fibre. Moreover, the consistency of the wavefield orientation, quantified using the notion of directional coherency, allows coherent arrivals to be identified and enhanced. In this work, we apply the monogenic signal to analyse submarine T-wave recordings following the magnitude 3.5 earthquake of 5 October 2023 in the western Alboran Sea, acquired along approximately 60 km of the Estepona-Tetouan fibre-optic cable. Directional coherency allows us to enhance coherent wave trains, attenuating the incoherent background while preserving their oscillatory structure. Combining the monogenic attributes, we track individual oscillations across the fibre, obtaining spatially consistent apparent-slowness estimates. Together with varying cable geometry, these estimates allow us to infer the incoming directions of two wave trains, revealing distinct backazimuths. We extend the methodology to direction-selective enhancement, revealing a weaker third wave train with opposite moveout that is obscured by stronger arrivals. Beyond these examples, we show that monogenic analysis offers new possibilites for wavefield comparison, with promising applications to lossy data compression and inversion. Our results highlight the versatility of monogenic analysis and its potential to become a central tool for interpreting DAS recordings.
item.dc:creator: Aleix Segui, Arantza Ugalde, Andreas Fichtner, Huynh Van Luong, Wes Armour

item.title: QuakeConsensus: Reducing false detections in automatic earthquake catalogs through consensus phase association
item.description: arXiv:2611.29891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic earthquake catalogs rely on phase associators to group the picks of a phase picker into events. Associators also produce false events that inflate the catalog. We measure the false events of five associators, PyOcto, GaMMA, REAL, GENIE, and backprojection, on two benchmarks built from observed phase picks in Taiwan. The first benchmark isolates 28,129 cataloged earthquakes in 20-minute windows, adding noise by shifting unassociated picks independently. The second evaluates 11,917 earthquakes from the 2024 $M_w$ 7.4 Hualien aftershock sequence, shifting unassociated P and S pairs together. We also propose a consensus association strategy that keeps an event found by at least two associators. With noise picks, single associators produce 5.3% to 10.2% false positives on the regional benchmark and 11.8% to 46.8% on the Hualien benchmark, whereas the consensus catalog reduces these false positive percentages to 4.2% and 11.5%, respectively. The consensus has the highest F1 score and the smallest percentage of false positives on both benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Wu-Yu Liao, En-Jui Lee

item.title: Conservative Rupture Force Relating Co-seismic Rupture and Afterslip Process
item.description: arXiv:2611.30324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The post-seismic phase plays a crucial role in the earthquake cycle by releasing co-seismic stress and reshaping the fault-zone stress field. Traditionally, the relationship between afterslip and co-seismic slip is made by the ratio of their respective moment ($R_M$). However, in this study, we perform numerical and theoretical analyses to reveal that $R_M$ is inherently unstable. To quantify the afterslip, we first introduce an inter-seismic "equilibrium state" as a reference from which the pure afterslip is separated, while the afterslip releases the co-seismic stress loading over the velocity-strengthening region after correcting for this equilibrium state. To define the relationship between co- and afterslips, we propose a novel physical quantity termed the "conservative rupture force" (CRF), which is defined as the area integration of co-seismic stress drop. The CRF is equal to the area integration of stress loading over an infinite fault plane as well as the area integration of afterslip stress release over an infinite time and fault plane. This relationship holds for both full-space and half-space faults. We derive a dimensionless parameter as the ratio between afterslip and co-seismic CRFs as $R_F$. We also propose a strategy to derive such a factor with given co-seismic and afterslip models. We demonstrate that after correcting for the spatial partitioning of stress release, $R_F$ converges to one in an infinite time. This strategy is applied to the 2015 Mw 7.8 Gorkha earthquake, and we find that afterslips released 30% of coseismic stress loading over 5.5 years after the mainshock, while a large portion of the fault plane remained locked. The introduction of the equilibrium state and CRF offers a fresh quantitative view to understand relationships between inter-, co- and post-seismic fault slips.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Hou, Zeyan Zhao, Han Yue

item.title: Non-intrusive Differentiation of High-Performance Seismic Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2611.30524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differentiable frameworks for seismic tomography compute model gradients without hand-derived adjoint sources. Some differentiate through wave propagation, which can be costly in time and memory at scale. Others use native adjoints with automatically constructed sources, and the efficiency is largely determined by forward and adjoint solves. Mature seismic solvers offer efficient, well-tested propagation, but a reusable workflow is still needed to connect them to user-defined misfit functions. Here we present a non-intrusive workflow and an Agent Skill for adapting existing seismic solvers to differentiable inversion. We apply automatic differentiation (AD) to the preprocessing and misfit, stopping backpropagation at the synthetic data. The solver injects this data derivative at the receivers to form the adjoint source, then computes the model gradient from the native forward and adjoint simulations. To assess accuracy and computational cost, we compared our hybrid implementation (HybridADFWI) with full AD in ADFWI using the same forward solver. Across six settings, the gradients agreed to within $1.4\times10^{-6}$ in relative $L_2$ norm. For one iteration, HybridADFWI was 2.4-4.6 times as fast as ADFWI and used 5-22% less peak reserved GPU memory. Guided by the Skill, a coding agent adds missing adjoint routines, verifies gradients, and runs recovery tests for user-selected model parameters. We applied the Skill to two independent solvers, building DiffSPECFEM2D and DiffAxiSEM3D. In the P-wave velocity tests, DiffSPECFEM2D recovered the main dipping layers of Marmousi-II, and DiffAxiSEM3D recovered the overall shape of the SEG/EAGE salt body. Both frameworks support user-defined misfits while preserving native kernels and parallel execution.
item.dc:creator: Xi Wang, Zhanwen Li, Xin Liu

item.title: ESM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Whether AI Agents Understand Earth System Model Physics and Code
item.description: arXiv:2611.28477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents that modify Earth System Model (ESM) code must preserve both software interfaces and the physical assumptions encoded in them. We introduce ESM-Bench, a benchmark of 60 developer-commit tasks from 6 repositories: Noah-MP, CLM5, SUMMA, ParFlow, MOM6, and VIC. The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. Each task includes a scientific objective, parent-commit source files, a reference diff, and three stored prompt variants. An artifact audit confirms that all 60 reference diffs apply to their supplied starting files. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.
item.dc:creator: Koutian Wu, Yuxuan Cao, Gengchen Mai, Zeping Liu

item.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
item.description: arXiv:2611.30198v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.
item.dc:creator: Parastoo Farajpoor, Mohammadreza Narimani

item.title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
item.description: arXiv:2611.31212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Omar Sallam, David Coe, Jeremy Feinstein, Hugo Torres, Sofia Sahagun Covarrubias, Eugene Yan

item.title: Resonant lunar tides of Earth's core and basal magma ocean
item.description: arXiv:2606.16340v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Earth's magnetic field is generated by fluid motion in the liquid-metal core and has been active for billions of years. However, prior to the onset of inner-core growth, the sources of mechanical power that drove the geodynamo remain uncertain. During this period, the core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean (BMO), creating two immiscible fluid layers separated by a density interface, beneath the solid mantle. We develop a theory for lunar tides in this core--BMO system, in which the tidal potential acts on the density contrast between the two layers. The resulting dynamics differ fundamentally from previous models driven by imposed deformation of the core's bounding envelope. In the inviscid limit, the response transitions from an equilibrium tide to an interfacial gravity wave as forcing frequency increases. The two regimes are separated by a resonance that occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency of the degree-2, order-2 interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, linking the problem to the theory of elliptical instability. Finite viscosity regularises the resonance, introduces phase lag and generates oscillatory boundary layers. Combined with parameterised models of lunar recession and BMO crystallisation, the theory predicts enhanced core-boundary ellipticity, core-flow speed, magnetic Reynolds number and instability metrics, particularly near resonance. These results identify a previously unexplored mechanism for tidally driven flow in differentiated planetary bodies and show that a BMO can enhance tidal coupling to the core, potentially contributing to dynamo action.
item.dc:creator: Murray B. C. Kiernan, Hamish C. F. C. Hay, David W. Rees Jones, James F. J. Bryson, Richard F. Katz

item.title: Seismic P- and S-wave attenuation inversion in time-frequency domain based on Kramers-Kronig relations
item.description: arXiv:2609.05922v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Seismic attenuation (inverse quality factor) inversion is important for gas reservoir prediction. Two key issues in seismic attenuation inversion are the development of a physically consistent reflection coefficient equation and stable inversion of seismic attenuation from seismic data. To address these issues, this study, within the framework of isotropic linear viscoelastic media, starts from the Kramers-Kronig relations and expresses the viscoelastic stiffness matrix as a function of seismic attenuation. Under the assumptions of weak attenuation and small elastic and attenuation contrasts across the interface, a frequency-dependent PP-wave reflection coefficient equation explicitly containing P- and S-wave attenuation terms is derived using scattering theory. The derived equation not only satisfies the causality constraint but also preserves a compact mathematical form. Based on this equation, P- and S-wave attenuation are estimated by a time-frequency domain Bayesian inversion. To improve resolution and stability, the inversion adopts a recursive frequency strategy with half-power overlapping Gaussian windows, in which the result at the previous frequency serves as the prior model for the next frequency, and prior models are built from well-log rock-physics modeling to provide low-frequency constraints. Synthetic seismic data tests show that the inversion resolution and accuracy improve as the inversion frequency increases and that the method remains robust at a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 dB. Application to field seismic data further demonstrates that the P-wave attenuation anomalies effectively identify gas reservoirs, whereas S-wave attenuation is insensitive to gas reservoirs. This study provides a new approach for extracting P- and S-wave attenuation information from seismic data and achieving high-resolution prediction of gas reservoirs.
item.dc:creator: Shengyi Wang, Xuehua Chen, Xingyu Luo, Kaixing Huang

item.title: Surface elevation errors in finite element Stokes models for glacier evolution
item.description: arXiv:2408.06470v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The primary data which determine the evolution of glaciation are the bedrock elevation and the surface mass balance. From this data, which we assume is defined over a fixed land region, the glacier's geometry solves a free boundary problem which balances the time derivative of the surface elevation, the surface velocity from the Stokes flow of the ice, and the surface mass balance rate. This problem can be posed in weak form as a variational inequality over a cone of admissible surface elevation functions, those which are above the bedrock topography. After some preparatory theory for the Stokes problem, we conjecture that the corresponding continuous-space, implicit time-step variational inequality problem is well-posed if the surface kinematical equation is appropriately regularized. This conjecture is supported by physical arguments and numerical evidence. We then prove a general theorem which bounds the numerical error made by finite element approximations of nonlinear-operator variational inequalities in Banach spaces. This bound is a sum of error terms of different types, special to variational inequalities. When it is applied to the implicit time-step glacier problem there are three terms in the bound: an error from discretizing the bed elevation primarily near the glacier margin, an error from numerically solving for the Stokes velocity, and finally a C\'ea-type best-approximation error for the finite element space representation of the surface elevation. The design of glacier models is then reconsidered based on this mostly a priori error analysis.
item.dc:creator: Ed Bueler

item.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2604.23874v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The differentiable physics paradigm may be leveraged as an a-posteriori approach for discovering turbulence closure models by embedding a neural network parameterization directly inside the solver and optimizing it given potentially sparse target data. This addresses a key limitation of a-priori learning where direct numerical simulation (DNS) data is used to approximate the subgrid stress with the assumption of a low-pass filter. Closures trained in this a-priori manner frequently lead to unstable deployments due to the mismatch between the assumed filter and the effect of numerical discretizations and coarse-graining. In comparison, while typically stable during deployment, a-posteriori learning incurs high computational costs due to the need to backpropagate through a large eddy simulation (LES) solver. Furthermore, a-posteriori methods are challenging to apply broadly since they require significant modification of existing solvers. Finally, both approaches are limited when generalization is desired across different numerical schemes with their implicit filtering characteristics. In this work, we present a deep-learning approach for turbulence closure modeling built on the continuous data assimilation framework. Our approach enables the a-priori training of closures using DNS data observed only at coarse-grid points without modifying or differentiating through the LES solver, while preserving stability during deployment for the recovery of long-term statistics. We focus on the model's ability to adapt to different discretizations by explicitly conditioning it on the numerical scheme. We use two- and three-dimensional canonical cases to test our framework and show that the learned correction systematically tracks the discretization error of the coarse solver.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Suriyanarayanan, Dibyajyoti Chakraborty, Romit Maulik

item.title: Connecting Microseismicity to Lithology via a Model of Slip Avalanches
item.description: arXiv:2607.06886v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fluid injection into the earth's crust can induce small and frequent earthquakes in the subsurface. Predicting their sizes and temporal occurrences via statistical analysis is crucial for safe operations in unconventional oil and gas recovery, enhanced geothermal systems, and geologic carbon storage. Here we show that a simple micromechanical model of slip avalanches in slowly deforming solids predicts the slip statistics observed over drastically different spatial scales, namely meter-scale microseismic observations and nanometer- to micrometer-scale nanoindentation experiments can be described with this model. Microseismic catalogs extracted from high-pressure fluid injection operations into geological basins with various lithologies and nanoindentation experiments on shale across a wide range of temperatures and mineral compositions yield statistics consistent with model predictions. This universality across materials, temperatures, and scales is consistent with the prediction that the slip statistics result from only a few basic properties. Previously debated deviations of the statistics in layered sedimentary formations are explained by finite-size and stress-integrative effects resulting from mechanically weak bedding planes. The slip statistics therefore provide important information about the structure and scales of the bedding planes. Conversely, the basin structure can also be used to predict the probability distribution for the sizes of triggered microseismic events.

item.title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
item.description: arXiv:2611.09854v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR instrument aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM for elevation matching. We ask whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Additionally fusing a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source substantially improved the accuracy. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single offset per ground track, then point by point. For most tracks, the per-track corrections nearly agreed with those from the airborne LiDAR DTM. Point-by-point corrections, however, did not agree. This was because the error of the generated DTM was close to the elevation differences that point-by-point correction must resolve, and most of this error lay at scales that even a 10 m-resolution DTM can represent. Under similar conditions, a super-resolved DTM may be usable in place of a 1 m-resolution DTM for per-track correction, but improving the accuracy, or using it for point-by-point correction as well, requires reducing the error at these scales rather than reproducing fine relief.
item.dc:creator: Natsuki Yuda, Shinichiro Shirota
